title: The stars, the moon, the sun, again
hookLine: Ibrahim's search returns in its full setting (6:74–79)

lines: A SON, A FATHER, A QUESTION.
cards: On day thirty-two, three hundred sixty-eight days ago, you met a young man looking up at a star, then the moon, then the sun, watching each one set. You heard him say: I love not things that set. That was one photo.

Today the Qur'an hands you the whole roll of film. In surah six, the star isn't where the story begins. It begins with an argument between a son and his father, and it ends with a question about who is truly safe.

teach.b: Verse seventy-four. Ibrahim says to his father, whom this verse calls Azar: do you take idols as gods? I see you and your people in plain error.
Commentators differ on the name Azar: some take it as his father's name, others as a title or another relative, since the Bible calls Abraham's father Terah.

teach.h: SHOWN THE KINGDOM OF THE HEAVENS.
teach.b: Verse seventy-five: Allah showed Ibrahim the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among those who are certain. Only then comes the night sky: the star, the moon, the sun, each one setting.
When the sun goes down, Ibrahim turns.
In Pickthall's words: “Lo! I have turned my face toward Him Who created the heavens and the earth,” upright by nature, not one of those who set up partners.
Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying it in the supplication that opened his prayer, right after the first Allahu akbar.

teach.h: WHO HAS MORE RIGHT TO SAFETY?
teach.b: Then his people argue, and he asks them: which of us has more right to feel safe? Me, who fears no idol, or you, who don't fear associating partners with God?
Verse eighty-two answers: those who believe and don't mix their faith with wrongdoing have safety. A hadith in Bukhari says that verse frightened the companions: which of us has never done wrong?
The Prophet explained that the wrong here means associating partners with God.

Verse eighty-three closes the scene: that was Our argument, which We gave Ibrahim against his people. So the stars were never just stargazing. They were Ibrahim's answer, given where everyone could see it: the sky.

how: Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet opening his prayer with a supplication that includes 6:79, I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, and some Muslims open their prayer with it today.

Ibrahim's search in full: idols, sky, a turned face

games.q: you hear verse 82: those who don't mix faith with wrongdoing have safety. you're a companion, and you're worried. what do you do?
o: ask the Prophet what the verse means.
games.why: the companions asked, and the Prophet explained that the wrong meant here is associating partners with God (Bukhari).

practice: Picture the last sunset you remember, and go back to day thirty-two: the star, the moon, the sun. What were you holding onto then that has since set, a worry, a plan, a person, a phone you loved?
If you pray, you can say Ibrahim's line, I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth; if not, let your eyes rest on the sky.

wordCard.voice: The stars. Ibrahim's search in its full setting: the argument with Azar, the kingdom of the heavens shown, the turning of the face, and the question of who is safe. Today's word.
